The rest of the profile centers on bodily pain, terror, injustice, contamination, and identity change following interpersonal assault, so these two triggers appear clinically incoherent with the formulation and with the other selected items.

vignette: Marcus is a 30-year-old African American man who works as a curriculum designer. He has been struggling with intense symptoms following physical abuse from his former romantic partner. The traumatic event left deep scars both physically and emotionally, which continue to affect various aspects of his life. The night Marcus was assaulted by his partner still haunts him in vivid detail. They had been arguing about family issues, and the tension escalated into a violent altercation. The smell of burnt food from the kitchen mingled with the pungent odor of alcohol, creating an overwhelming sensory experience that he has never been able to shake off. Since then, Marcus finds himself triggered by comments about family dynamics or catching even a whiff of alcohol, which immediately transport him back to that painful night. The olfactory cues are especially potent; when he smells burnt food, it's as if the assault is happening all over again. He recalls feeling the same physical pain in his body and experiencing overwhelming terror—the same feelings that were present during the event. These memories replay with such intensity that he often feels like he’s back in that moment of horror. The triggers have also led to a cascade of negative appraisals about himself and his situation. Marcus is deeply convinced that what happened was deeply unfair, and no justice has been served for him. He believes that the person he has become since the assault is unrecognizable to himself, feeling as if he carries the weight of contamination from the abuse. This sense of contamination permeates every aspect of his life, leaving him feeling dirty and unworthy. In his role as a curriculum designer, Marcus often finds himself in meetings where family dynamics are discussed as part of educational programs. These discussions trigger memories of that night, bringing back the same physical pain and terror he felt then. He tries to avoid these situations but finds it increasingly difficult to do so without drawing attention to his absences or avoidance behaviors. The more he is triggered by these sensory cues, the stronger the negative appraisals become. His sense of self-worth diminishes as he grapples with feeling unrecognizable and tainted. This has led him to withdraw from social situations and isolate himself, further reinforcing his belief that what happened was unjust and left no room for recovery. What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a combination of the relentless triggers at work and the overwhelming sense of injustice that kept him trapped in a cycle of distress. He is most afraid that he will never be able to shake off the memories and the physical pain they bring, but also hopes that with support, he can regain some semblance of normalcy and peace.
